content.text:
Short answer: our Jira connector is read-only today; Atlassian’s MCP gives us the missing Jira and Confluence write capabilities, but it is not quite plug-and-play with Lobu yet.

I verified production just now:

- Jira is installed and connected.
- It exposes the `issues` feed for live JQL reads.
- `operations.listAvailable({ connector_key: "jira" })` returns **0 operations**.
- The connector requests read and webhook scopes, not `write:jira-work`; there are no create, edit, transition, or comment actions in [jira.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/connectors/src/jira.ts:286).

Atlassian’s hosted Rovo MCP for Cloud is much broader:

- Jira: search/get, create/edit, transition, comment, and worklogs.
- Confluence: read/search, create/update pages, and create comments.
- It does not expose every conceivable mutation; for example, deletion isn’t in the current supported tool list. [Atlassian supported tools](https://support.atlassian.com/atlassian-rovo-mcp-server/docs/supported-tools/)

Lobu already has the correct architectural seam: remote MCP servers can be wrapped as connectors and their tools become governed operations, with writes pessimistically approval-gated. The catch is authentication:

- Our `mcp_url` installer probes the server anonymously and creates `authSchema: null`.
- Atlassian’s endpoint rejects anonymous initialization with `401`—I confirmed that live.
- Atlassian currently expects interactive OAuth 2.1 at `https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp/authv2`, or an admin-enabled API token for headless workloads. [OAuth setup](https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/rovo-mcp/guides/getting-started/), [API-token setup](https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/rovo-mcp/guides/configuring-authentication-via-api-token/)

My recommendation: add an `atlassian-rovo` MCP-backed connector using the existing connector/operations contract, with protected-resource OAuth discovery and authenticated tool discovery. Keep the native Jira connector for feeds, webhooks, durable events, and Behaviors; use Rovo MCP for rich Jira/Confluence reads and mutations. That avoids rebuilding Atlassian’s tool surface while preserving Lobu approvals and audit. No new agent-facing API should be needed—just the authentication adapter and connector packaging.

No—not end to end from only adding `mcpConfig`. The connector-to-MCP composition is real, but Atlassian exposes gaps in our current implementation.

What already works:

- `mcpConfig` discovers upstream tools and converts them into Lobu operations.
- Execution uses the selected connection and flows through Lobu runs, approvals, and auditing.

What currently prevents a reliable Atlassian integration:

1. **OAuth resource mismatch.** The existing Jira connection obtains a token for `api.atlassian.com`. Rovo MCP advertises itself as the distinct resource `https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp/authv2`. MCP requires the `resource` parameter in both authorization and token requests, and servers must reject tokens issued for another audience. [MCP authorization requirements](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/authorization)

   Lobu can add `resource` to the authorization URL through `authParams`, but its token exchange currently cannot send it; see [oauth-providers.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/connect/oauth-providers.ts:159).

2. **One connection, two credential audiences.** The native Jira feed/webhook needs an Atlassian REST token, while Rovo MCP needs an MCP-specific token. The MCP proxy currently reuses the connection’s single OAuth account credential in [credential-resolver.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/mcp-proxy/credential-resolver.ts:29). Replacing it with an MCP token could then break the native feed.

Atlassian explicitly changes the visible tool set based on the user’s products and granted scopes, so multiple Atlassian accounts could receive the wrong operation catalog. [Atlassian OAuth behavior](https://support.atlassian.com/atlassian-rovo-mcp-server/docs/configuring-oauth-2-1/)

- Keep `jira` for native feeds, webhooks, and durable Behavior inputs.
- Add a bundled `atlassian-rovo` connector that extends the official MCP through `mcpConfig`.
- Give it its own MCP OAuth connection.
- First complete protected-resource OAuth discovery/resource binding, JSON+SSE transport, and connection-scoped tool discovery.

content.text:
Yes—this is a meaningful product gap, but Lobu already has much of the foundation.

Today Lobu supports managed OAuth reuse:

- Lobu Cloud retains the OAuth app secret and the user’s refresh token.
- A local Lobu instance declares `managedBy`, authenticates through `lobu login`, and fetches only the user’s current access token.
- The Cloud-side connection is consent-only, so feeds execute locally and provider data is not duplicated in Cloud. See [cloud-credential.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/connect/cloud-credential.ts:4) and [connection-token-route.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/connect/connection-token-route.ts:124).

Lobu also has `app_installations` and gateway-side installation-token minting, but actual token minting is currently implemented only for GitHub, and it is not exposed as a general Cloud-to-local delegation mechanism. See [installation-token-provider.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/installation/installation-token-provider.ts:35) and [registry.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/installation/registry.ts:19).

So the gap is:

| Credential type | Local reuse today |
|---|---|
| User OAuth via `managedBy` | Yes |
| GitHub App token inside Lobu’s runtime | Yes |
| Cloud app-installation token delegated to separate local Lobu | No |
| Resource-bound upstream MCP OAuth | No |
| Atlassian Rovo end-to-end | No |

For Atlassian specifically, Rovo should not be modeled as one shared Jira installation token. Atlassian uses user-driven OAuth 2.1 and explicitly states that tokens are not shared between users. Lobu can provide the hosted OAuth application, but every user must grant their own Jira/Confluence permissions. [Atlassian OAuth documentation](https://support.atlassian.com/atlassian-rovo-mcp-server/docs/configuring-oauth-2-1/)

I’d productize this as “Cloud-managed connections”:

1. Lobu Cloud hosts the provider app registration.
2. The customer installs the app or grants personal consent.
3. Local Lobu references it through `managedBy`.
4. At execution time:

   - Default for MCP and writes: local Lobu calls a Cloud capability proxy; no provider token leaves Cloud.
   - When execution genuinely must happen locally: Cloud issues a short-lived, audience-scoped lease to the local gateway—not to the agent worker.
   - Durable credentials such as app private keys or Slack bot tokens remain proxy-only.

The lease/capability must be bound to the exact user, organization, connection, site/installation, OAuth resource, scopes, agent/run, and expiry, with revocation and auditing. The existing `/oauth/connection-token` contract is too narrow because it identifies only `{ org, connector_key }` and supports only the caller’s consent-only OAuth connection.

So: yes, “connect once through Lobu Cloud, run safely anywhere—including locally” is a real product opportunity. It is not a greenfield auth project; it is the missing bridge joining `managedBy`, `app_installations`, and connector `mcpConfig`. For Jira/Confluence, that bridge also needs the MCP protected-resource OAuth and Streamable HTTP fixes identified earlier.

Yes. If “local” means a local runtime paired with Lobu Cloud, it is fundamentally the same architecture as GitHub. I overstated the platform gap.

GitHub already does:

`Cloud app installation → short-lived installation token → credential lease → local/remote runtime`

The app private key remains in Cloud; only the derived token reaches the authorized runtime. That machinery is in [credential-lease.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/agent-tooling/credential-lease.ts:103).

Atlassian should reuse that model, with one distinction: Rovo MCP normally uses a per-user OAuth grant, not one organization-wide installation token. Atlassian explicitly says tokens must not be shared between users. So it becomes:

`Cloud-hosted Lobu OAuth app → each user consents → resource-bound access token → MCP proxy/local gateway`

The actual remaining work is therefore:

- Add the bundled `atlassian-rovo` connector with Jira + Confluence `mcpConfig`.
- Reuse `managedBy` for Cloud-held user grants.
- Extend OAuth exchange for the MCP `resource` audience.
- Make the MCP client fully support Streamable HTTP/SSE.
- Make tool discovery connection-specific.
- Preserve GitHub-style tenant isolation and explicit installation transfer.

So I’d classify it as an **Atlassian connector/provider coverage gap**, not a new Lobu product primitive. We should reuse the existing Cloud-managed credential and lease system, not build another credential broker.

Only if “local” means a completely standalone Lobu control plane that is not logged into or paired with Lobu Cloud would there be a separate Cloud-to-local delegation gap.

Separate at the credential/runtime layer—not necessarily as two unrelated things in the UI.

The existing `jira` connector and Rovo MCP do different jobs:

| Capability | Native `jira` | Atlassian Rovo MCP |
|---|---|---|
| JQL feeds and durable ingestion | Yes | No |
| Jira webhooks | Yes | No |
| Create/edit/transition issues | No | Yes |
| Confluence operations | No | Yes |
| Authentication target | `api.atlassian.com` | `mcp.atlassian.com/.../authv2` |

We cannot simply attach `mcpConfig` to `jira` because one Lobu connection currently owns one OAuth grant:

1. Sending the existing Jira API token to Rovo risks rejection because it was minted for a different protected resource.
2. Changing Jira to mint a Rovo token would risk breaking its direct Jira API sync and webhook operations.
3. Storing both grants inside one connection would introduce a new multi-credential connector model, persistence contract, and lifecycle—not a small extension.

We also should not move or replace native Jira with Rovo. That would discard the valuable part of our connector: continuous JQL ingestion and webhooks. Rovo provides agent-invoked tools, not a durable synchronization replacement.

My recommendation is:

- Keep `jira` unchanged for feeds, webhooks, and durable Jira context.
- Add `atlassian.rovo` for Jira and Confluence MCP operations.
- Present both under an “Atlassian” family in product UX later, so it feels cohesive.
- Eventually offer a combined installation flow that creates the two underlying connections. Internally they should still retain separate OAuth grants.

The supporting changes are needed because:

- `resource?: string` ensures Lobu requests and refreshes a token specifically valid for Rovo.
- JSON plus SSE handling is required for proper MCP Streamable HTTP interoperability.
- Connection-scoped discovery prevents one Atlassian account’s available tools/sites/scopes from being cached and shown for another account.
- Cloud-to-local token reuse itself already exists; we only need the Rovo connection to participate in that existing managed OAuth path.

So the architectural gap is not “Jira should become Rovo.” It is that Lobu currently supports durable Jira ingestion but lacks the complementary Atlassian operational tool surface. I recommend proceeding with the separate backend connector plus the additive OAuth `resource` field.

I’m checking the exact mismatch between that model and Lobu’s current `mcpConfig`, because the key question is whether it supports a second MCP login or only reuses the connector’s existing token.

The important distinction is emerging: “the Jira connector can support actions” is true; “today’s `mcpConfig` can ask the user for a second upstream login” is false. You’re right: the Jira connector can support the actions. My separate-connector proposal was the smallest backend change, not an inherent product requirement.

The mismatch is in today’s `mcpConfig` implementation.

### What happens today

1. The user connects Jira.
2. Lobu performs Jira 3LO OAuth with `audience=api.atlassian.com`.
3. One user token is attached to the connection.
4. Native Jira feeds and webhooks use that token.

If we merely add:

```ts
mcpConfig: {
  upstreamUrl: "https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp/authv2"
}
```

Lobu does not start another OAuth login. `mcpConfig` currently contains only `upstreamUrl`, and the proxy automatically sends the connection’s existing token. See [connector-types.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/connector-sdk/src/connector-types.ts:65) and [credential-resolver.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/mcp-proxy/credential-resolver.ts:29).

That produces:

```text
Jira login
  └─ token for api.atlassian.com
       ├─ native Jira feeds ✅
       └─ sent to Rovo MCP ❓ wrong protected resource
```

Atlassian’s normal Jira 3LO flow targets `api.atlassian.com`, while Rovo’s OAuth flow targets the Rovo MCP protected resource. It is the same Atlassian user, but potentially a different resource-bound grant and access token. [Jira 3LO documentation](https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/jira/software/oauth-2-3lo-apps/), [Rovo OAuth documentation](https://support.atlassian.com/atlassian-rovo-mcp-server/docs/configuring-oauth-2-1/).

### What you are proposing

We should let a connector declare authentication specifically for its upstream MCP:

```ts
mcpConfig: {
  upstreamUrl: "https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp/authv2",
  auth: {
    type: "oauth",
    provider: "atlassian",
    resource: "https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp/authv2",
    requiredScopes: [/* Jira + Confluence scopes */]
  }
}
```

Then installation becomes:

```text
One Jira/Atlassian connection
  ├─ primary OAuth grant → native Jira feeds and webhooks
  └─ MCP OAuth grant     → Rovo Jira and Confluence actions
```

The user still logs in with their own Atlassian account. Lobu Cloud supplies the managed app credentials, stores and refreshes that user’s grants, and the local Lobu runtime obtains only the appropriate short-lived token.

To support this properly, Lobu needs:

- `mcpConfig.auth` in the connector SDK.
- OAuth `resource` propagation.
- A typed secondary credential binding on a connection; today a connection has only one user OAuth profile.
- Installation continuation for “authorize actions.”
- Cloud-to-local token resolution by credential slot.
- Connection-specific MCP discovery and JSON/SSE transport support.

For Jira actions alone, we could instead add native `create/edit/comment/transition` actions using the existing Jira REST token and request `write:jira-work`. That is simpler, but it does not give us Confluence or the general “extend a connector with an authenticated MCP” capability.

My revised recommendation: keep the existing `jira` key and feeds, extend that logical connector with authenticated Rovo MCP actions, and present it as Atlassian/Jira + Confluence. No separate connector card. The real product change is teaching `mcpConfig` to own its upstream user authorization instead of assuming the primary connector token works everywhere.

Today Lobu only supports:

```ts
mcpConfig: {
  upstreamUrl: string
}
```

But its behavior is incomplete:

1. Resolve the connector’s existing OAuth token.
2. Send that token upstream.
3. If unavailable, try unauthenticated.
4. On `401`, stop.

It does not parse the MCP OAuth challenge or initiate another user authorization. See [connector-types.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/connector-sdk/src/connector-types.ts:65) and [client.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/mcp-proxy/client.ts:205).

A compliant flow should be:

```text
upstreamUrl
  → unauthenticated initialize
  → 401 + WWW-Authenticate
  → protected-resource metadata
  → authorization-server metadata
  → client registration
  → user OAuth + PKCE
  → connection-bound MCP token
  → tools/list
```

The current MCP specification explicitly requires clients to discover protected-resource and authorization-server metadata and include the discovered `resource` in authorization and token requests. [MCP authorization specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization).

Atlassian publishes everything needed:

- Rovo protected resource
- Atlassian authorization server
- authorization and token endpoints
- PKCE support
- client-ID metadata and dynamic-registration support

So for Atlassian, those should not be hardcoded in `mcpConfig.auth`.

What discovery cannot decide is Lobu’s permission policy. Atlassian advertises every supported scope—including Jira, Confluence, Compass, and Teamwork Graph. Lobu should not request all of them automatically. We likely need only a scope allowlist:

```ts
mcpConfig: {
  upstreamUrl: "https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp/authv2",
  requestedScopes: [
    "read:me",
    "read:account",
    "read:jira-work",
    "write:jira-work",
    "search:jira-work",
    // selected Confluence scopes
  ]
}
```

Endpoints, resource, PKCE, and registration remain discovered.

### How big?

This is a medium-to-large platform feature, not a Jira edit:

- Generic MCP OAuth discovery and validation.
- Client registration/identity support.
- Browser authorization and callback continuation.
- Durable secondary-token binding to the same connection.
- Refresh and revocation lifecycle.
- Managed cloud-to-local token issuance for that credential slot.
- Connection-scoped tool discovery.
- SSE/JSON Streamable HTTP fixes.
- Jira metadata and end-to-end tests.

Roughly 15–25 touched files and perhaps 1,500–3,000 lines including tests. I would split it into two or three PRs:

1. Generic MCP transport and OAuth discovery.
2. Durable connection-bound MCP authorization plus managed local reuse.
3. Enable Rovo on the existing Jira connector.

The largest design decision is how a connection durably binds an additional MCP OAuth grant. Discovery solves where and how to authenticate; it does not solve where Lobu associates and manages that second user credential. ### What GitHub actually does

GitHub does not use `mcpConfig` or an upstream GitHub MCP server.

It has:

- Native actions implemented inside [github.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/connectors/src/github.ts:734): create issues, comments, PRs, merge PRs, etc.
- Those actions call GitHub’s REST API using the connection credential.
- GitHub App installations let Lobu mint short-lived installation tokens.
- Local agents receive those tokens as `GH_TOKEN` through [credential-lease.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/agent-tooling/credential-lease.ts:104).

So GitHub follows:

```text
GitHub App installation
  → Lobu mints installation token
  ├─ native connector actions
  └─ local GH_TOKEN for gh CLI
```

There is no upstream MCP authentication involved.

### What `mcpConfig` currently supports

The public contract is only:

```ts
mcpConfig?: {
  upstreamUrl: string;
}
```

The connector MCP proxy then loads the connection’s primary `auth_profile_id` and sends that existing token upstream. It does not parse `WWW-Authenticate`, discover protected-resource metadata, register an OAuth client, or launch another login.

Lobu does have related OAuth machinery, but for different directions:

- MCP clients authenticating to Lobu.
- Lobu users authenticating through an external identity provider.
- Ordinary connector OAuth.
- GitHub installation-token leases.

None is wired into Lobu acting as an OAuth client of a connector’s upstream MCP.

### Why Jira is different

If we copy GitHub’s approach, Jira actions are straightforward:

```text
Jira OAuth token
  → Jira REST API
  ├─ existing feeds/webhooks
  └─ native create/edit/comment/transition actions
```

That is a relatively small change: expand/re-consent for `write:jira-work`, implement the native actions, and test approval/execution. Probably around 3–6 production/test files and several hundred lines.

Rovo is different:

```text
Existing Jira token → api.atlassian.com
Rovo MCP token      → mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp/authv2
```

The MCP authorization specification forbids sending a token to a resource for which it was not issued. Therefore, using Rovo requires Lobu to discover and manage another resource-bound grant. [MCP authorization specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization).

So the corrected framing is:

- “Give Jira GitHub-like write actions”: small, use native REST, no MCP change.
- “Extend Jira with Rovo so it also gains Confluence and every Rovo tool”: medium-large generic authenticated-MCP feature.
- “GitHub already proves cloud credentials can be reused locally”: yes.
- “GitHub proves connector MCP OAuth discovery works”: no, because GitHub never exercises that path.

My recommendation is to add native Jira actions now, matching GitHub, while treating authenticated upstream MCP discovery as the separate reusable platform feature needed for Rovo and Confluence.

I’m applying the Lobu connector boundary here because “consistent” has two meanings: a consistent agent-facing operation model versus a consistent credential/runtime implementation. MCP helps the first and future integrations; it adds real moving parts to the second.

Short answer: MCP is more extensible and consistent across providers, but it is not more reliable for core Jira writes today. It introduces additional failure modes.

| Concern | Native Jira REST actions | Rovo MCP |
|---|---|---|
| Network path | Lobu → Jira | Lobu → Rovo → Jira |
| Authentication | Existing Jira grant | Additional resource-bound MCP grant |
| Operation schemas | Controlled by us | Dynamically controlled by Atlassian |
| Tool availability | Stable | Varies by scopes, products and admin policy |
| Retry/reconciliation | We can design per action | Lost write responses are unsafe to replay |
| New capabilities | We implement each one | Atlassian exposes them automatically |
| Confluence | Requires more native code | Included naturally |

MCP’s major benefit is marginal cost: once Lobu has generic authenticated-upstream MCP support, adding another compatible service becomes mostly an `upstreamUrl` plus permission policy.

But agent-facing consistency does not require every operation to be implemented through MCP. Lobu already normalizes native actions and MCP tools into the same operations and approval system.

My recommendation:

- Keep Jira feeds and webhooks native.
- Add the important Jira mutations natively: create, edit, comment and transition.
- Build authenticated MCP as a reusable platform capability for Confluence and Atlassian’s long-tail tools.
- Hide or deprioritize duplicate Rovo Jira tools when a stronger native operation exists.
- Never make core Jira writes depend exclusively on Rovo until its auth, schemas, availability and failure semantics have proven stable.

That gives us:

```text
Jira connector
  ├─ native feeds/webhooks
  ├─ reliable native Jira actions
  └─ discovered Rovo extensions
       ├─ Confluence
       └─ long-tail Atlassian tools
```

So: MCP is worth building if Lobu intends to extend several connectors from hosted MCP servers. For Jira writes alone, it would complicate the system without improving reliability. The strongest design is native critical paths plus MCP extensions.

The existing installer is usable, but four changes are needed for the complete cloud → local Rovo flow.

### 1. Complete Streamable HTTP support

Current connector MCP requests send only:

```http
Accept: application/json
```

and call `response.json()`. I reproduced the failure: a valid SSE MCP response throws `SyntaxError: Failed to parse JSON`.

Change:

- Send `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream`.
- Share one neutral parser between the gateway MCP proxy and connector MCP proxy.
- Parse SSE frames until the JSON-RPC response matching the request ID arrives.
- Handle `202` empty responses for notifications.
- Preserve the existing no-replay rule for ambiguous writes.

This is required by the [MCP Streamable HTTP specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/transports).

### 2. Make MCP discovery and credentials connection-specific

Currently:

- `tools/call` uses the selected connection.
- `tools/list` resolves the most recently updated connection for the connector.
- Its cache is keyed by organization + connector, not connection.
- Explicit operation execution can consequently validate against another account’s tool catalog.

More importantly, MCP bypasses `resolveExecutionAuth()`. That means a local `managedBy` connection—which deliberately has no local OAuth profile—cannot obtain its Lobu Cloud token for MCP calls.

Change:

- Route MCP credential resolution through `resolveExecutionAuth()`.
- Pass `connectionId` through `listOperations → buildConnectorOperations → discoverTools`.
- Key tool and session caches by organization + connector + connection.
- Ensure explicit list/execute paths surface authentication or discovery failures.
- Broad connector summaries may degrade per connector, but execution must not report a transport failure as “invalid operation.”

### 3. Round-trip dynamic MCP definitions through `lobu init`

`lobu init --from-org` currently exports managed connections but explicitly does not export organization-owned connector definitions. That works for bundled Gmail/GitHub connectors; it does not work for a connector installed from `mcp_url`.

Change:

- Include non-secret `mcp_config` in the installed-connector catalog response.
- Map it in the CLI’s remote connector representation.
- For an organization-installed MCP connector, generate a small local connector file:

```ts
export default defineConnector({
  key: "mcp.mcp-atlassian-com",
  name: "Atlassian Rovo",
  authSchema: { /* endpoints and resource, no credentials */ },
  mcpConfig: {
    upstreamUrl: "https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp/authv2",
  },
});
```

- Add it through the existing `connectorFromFile()` mechanism.

This keeps the refresh token and OAuth client credentials in Lobu Cloud while giving local Lobu the definition needed to discover and execute Rovo tools. No new connector framework is needed.

### 4. Pin a local connection to the exact cloud grant

The current managed-token request contains only `org + connector_key`. If one user has two Rovo grants, the database query can return either one.

Recommended additive contract:

```ts
managedBy: {
  org: "lobu-cloud",
  connectionSlug: "my-atlassian-rovo"
}
```

The cloud request becomes:

```json
{
  "org": "lobu-cloud",
  "connector_key": "mcp.mcp-atlassian-com",
  "connection_slug": "my-atlassian-rovo"
}
```

Older unpinned configurations can remain supported when exactly one grant exists; multiple matches should fail with an explicit ambiguity error.

This is the only meaningful public SDK/API design change. Adding `mcp_config` to the existing catalog response is also an additive response-contract change. Neither requires a database migration.

### What does not need changing

- The native Jira connector stays intact.
- No secondary OAuth slot is added to Jira.
- The existing Rovo OAuth discovery, DCR, PKCE, resource audience, refresh, approvals, and cloud token endpoint remain.
- Scope selection is not a blocker: when a challenge omits `scope`, requesting `scopes_supported` is the MCP-specified fallback. [MCP authorization specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization)
